## Detailed analysis of context selectivity

We start clarifying how context selectivity increases over learning. Results from simulations, and numerical integration of Equation 125, indicate that context selectivity increases for the synaptic drive, ks; this increase is then reflected in the activity, ys (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). In this section, we analyze the behaviour of context selectivity for the synaptic drive. Focussing on the synaptic drive, instead of activity, allows us to derive results analytically. In the following, we start from Equation 125 and show that, for the synaptic drive ks, the value of S~ctx increases over learning. At the end of this section, we comment on the insights provided by such derivation.

We start by simplifying the sums over trials contained in Equation 125, which involve pairs of trials s⁢s′ from the same, or different context. ## Extracting intuition

Can we derive a more intuitive picture of why and how context selectivity increases over learning? We have seen in the previous paragraphs that context selectivity increases because the difference within the first set of curly parenthesis of Equation 141 is positive (while the difference within the second set of curly parenthesis vanishes). To simplify the math, we assume that cA=-cB; this condition thus reads:(160)⟨Δki11Δki22⟩i−⟨Δki11Δki(Q^+1)(Q^+1)⟩i>0.

(With respect to Equation 142, we could get rid of pairs of trials with s=((Q^+1)⁢1) because, when cA=-cB, they give identical results to s=(11).)

Equation 160 indicates that, over learning, activity from trial s=(11) becomes closer (i.e., more correlated) to activity from trials with the same category and context, such as s′=(22), than trials with the same category but different context, such as s′=((Q^+1)⁢(Q^+1)). On the contrary, activity from trial s=(11) becomes equally close to activity from trials with different category and same context, such as s′=((Q^+1)⁢2), and trials with different category and different context, such as s′=(2⁢(Q^+1)). This can be seen from Equation 159, from which (161)⟨Δki11Δki(Q^+1)2⟩i−⟨Δki11Δki2(Q^+1)⟩i=0

follows.

The geometrical relationships implied by both Equation 160 and Equation 161 can be easily verified in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, which shows the synaptic drive from simulated circuits; the middle panel shows a circuit for which we have exactly cA=-cB. Taken together, Equation 160 and Equation 161 indicate that the increase in context selectivity comes from activity clustering by context over learning; such clustering is, however, category dependent. This leads to the emergence of four statistically distinguishable clouds, one for each combination of category and context. This is visible in simulated activity from Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, and is illustrated in Figure 7A–C.

## Detailed analysis of category selectivity

We now provide extra detail on the behaviour of category selectivity. We start explaining why, as observed in Figure 6A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, initial selectivity does not vanish, but is weakly negative. This phenomenon is observed both for the synaptic drive ks and the activity ys; for the sake of simplicity, we focus on the former.

Consider for a moment the case Q=2 (XOR computation). The geometry of the initial synaptic drive is in that case particularly simple, and is illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D. As can be easily verified by using Equation 5b and Equation 110, each synaptic drive is given by the linear superposition of two vectors: a vector among μ~1 and μ~2, and a vector among ν~1 and ν~2. Vectors μ~ and ν~ are obtained by applying the initial connectivity u0 to vectors μ and ν (Equation 110); for example, μ~1=u0⋅μ1. In the plane spanned by vectors μ~ and ν~, the geometry of synaptic drives is square like (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D). To verify that, observe that the squared distance between consecutive vertices is identical – for example,(162)⟨(k0,i11−k0,i12)2⟩i=2⟨(k0,i11)2⟩i−2⟨k0,i11k0,i12⟩i=2−1=1

where we used Equation 43 together with Equation 111. Opposite vertices have instead double squared distance – for example,(163)⟨(k0,i11−k0,i22)2⟩i=2⟨(k0,i11)2⟩i−2⟨k0,i11k0,i22⟩i=2−0=2

as expected for a square. Importantly, consecutive vertices are associated with different categories, while opposite vertices are associated with the same category; this implies that initial category selectivity is negative. In fact, using Equation 162 and Equation 163 into Equation 124 yields:(164)S~cat=1−21+2=−13<0.

It is easy to see that initial category selectivity is negative also when Q>2. However, its magnitude converges to zero as the number of stimuli and context cues, Q, increases (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). This is due to the fact that, as Q becomes large, both the within-category and the across-category averages in Equation 124 become dominated by pairs of trials with different stimulus and context cue; activity from those pairs of trials are characterized by identical initial distances (=2, as in Equation 163), and thus the two averages become similar.

We now shed light on a second phenomenon: the fact that category selectivity increases over learning for the activity ys, but remains identical for the synaptic drive ks. This is observed both in simulations (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), and in numerical integration of theoretical expressions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). To see why this happens, we assume that the number of stimuli and context cues, Q, is fairly large (1≪Q≪N). As discussed above, in this limit, initial category selectivity is approximately close to zero. To compute selectivity after learning, we use Equation 124, and evaluate the within-category and the across-category averages. We compute averages to the dominant terms in Q, which correspond to pairs of trials with different stimulus and context cue. Using the same s and s′ trials as in Section Detailed analysis of context selectivity, we obtain(165)⟨⟨(kis−kis′)2⟩i⟩s,s′ same cat≃⟨(ki11−ki22)2⟩i+⟨(ki11−ki(Q^+1)(Q^+1))2⟩i+⟨(ki(Q^+1)1−ki(Q^+2)2)2⟩i+⟨(ki(Q^+1)1−ki1(Q^+1))2⟩i⟨⟨(kis−kis′)2⟩i⟩s,s′ diff cat≃⟨(ki11−ki(Q^+1)2)2⟩i+⟨(ki11−ki2(Q^+1))2⟩i+⟨(ki(Q^+1)1−ki12)2⟩i+⟨(ki(Q^+1)1−ki(Q^+2)(Q^+1))2⟩i.

To show that category selectivity does not change over learning, we need to show that the two lines above are identical. Using Equation 139, this condition can be written as:(166)⟨Δki11Δki22⟩i+⟨Δki11Δki(Q^+1)(Q^+1)⟩i+⟨Δki(Q^+1)1Δki(Q^+2)2⟩i+⟨Δki(Q^+1)1Δki1(Q^+1)⟩i=⟨Δki11Δki(Q^+1)2⟩i+⟨Δki11Δki2(Q^+1)⟩i+⟨Δki(Q^+1)1Δki12⟩i+⟨Δki(Q^+1)1Δki(Q^+2)(Q^+1)⟩i,

which can now be easily verified by using Equation 158 and Equation 159.

Equation 166 indicates that, on average across contexts, synaptic drives from trials with the same category are as close as trials with different category. This geometrical relationship can be easily verified in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, which shows the synaptic drive from simulated circuits. We focus on the middle panel, where we have cA=-cB. The four activity clouds corresponding to different combinations of category and context values are approximately arranged on the vertices of a square; consecutive vertices are associated with different categories, while opposite vertices are associated with the same category. To see why Equation 166 holds, note that squared distances among synaptic drives associated with different category are approximately identical, while squared distances among synaptic drives associated within the same category are either 0 (approximately, half of the times), or twice the across-category distance (the other half). It is interesting to observe that this square-like configuration, which emerges over learning from an almost unstructured one (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, left), strongly resembles the initial configuration of the XOR task (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).

A fundamental feature of this configuration is that synaptic drives are not linearly separable by category. The activity vectors ys, on the other hand, are linearly separable. Before learning, linear separability is guaranteed by the nonlinearity Ψ, which makes activity vectors linearly separable along random directions (Barak et al., 2013). After learning, activity vectors become linearly separable also along task-relevant directions. In the simplified scenario where ηw≪ηu, the activity vectors become linearly separable along w0; in the general case, they become linearly separable along a direction that is correlated with w0. This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D the configuration of activity is very similar to synaptic drives, but activity vectors associated with different categories clusters, and thus become linearly separable, along an emerging, orthogonal direction. This drives the increase in category selectivity that was observed both in equations and simulations (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). A further insight on the relationship between selectivity and activity geometry is given in the next section.

We conclude with a remark. Although for activity variables category selectivity robustly increases, the fact that selectivity is weakly negative before learning implies that asymptotic values can be small, or even negative. This is compatible with findings in Bernardi et al., 2020, where very small values of category clustering (Equation 124) were observed. This observation stresses the importance of measuring, in experimental preparations, neural activity across multiple stages of learning.

## Analysis of patterns of context and category selectivity

In this section, we investigate how changes in context and category selectivity are distributed across neurons.

In the simple task, we found that the magnitude of selectivity changes for a given neuron, i, was correlated with the magnitude of the ith entry of the initial readout vector w0 (Equation 65, Figure 5B, C). This vector defines the direction along which clustering by category takes place. In fact, if one draws the vector joining the centers of the activity clouds associated with different categories, yA and yB (Equation 78), the resulting direction is correlated with w0 (Equation 96). This direction is indicated with d in the main text; cloud centers yA and yB are plotted, in Figure 3B, C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, as magenta triangles.

In analogy with the simple task, we now hypothesize that the magnitude of changes in context and category selectivity for a given neuron, i, is related to the magnitude of the ith entry of the context and category directions, dctx and dcat. Those coincide with the directions along which clustering to context and category emerges (Figure 7B, C), and are given by the vectors joining the centers of the activity clouds associated with different contexts (Equation 130) and categories (Equation 78). The cloud centers for category and context are plotted, in Figure 7B, C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D, as magenta and pink triangles. This assumption is verified in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, B, which shows that selectivity changes and context and category directions are highly correlated. Our reasoning implies that, in order to understand how selectivity changes are distributed across neurons, we need to evaluate the entries of the context and category directions; this is done, analytically, in the rest of this section.

## Software

## Circuit simulations

Simulations were implemented with the Python programming language. Gradient-descent learning was implemented with the PyTorch package. We used the SGD optimization function, with loss MSELoss. On every learning epoch, the batch included all sensory input vectors. Training stopped when the loss function dropped below 10-5. Learning rates were taken to be η=0.1 for input connectivity u, and η⋅ηw/ηu (with values of ηu and ηw as indicated in Section Tables of parameters) for readout connectivity w.

Our editorial process produces two outputs: i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Evolution of neural activity in circuits bridging sensory and abstract knowledge" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 2 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Joshua Gold as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Guillaume Hennequin (Reviewer #1).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1) Justification of some of the model choices that the reviewers asked about and discussion of how much the results depend on them (especially the use of gradient descent).

2) More intuitive explanations for some of the mathematical statements to help make the paper more accessible for the majority of eLife readers.

3) A longer discussion about how this paper fits into the current literature, and how it can be generalised.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

We do have a couple of concerns which we would recommend adding some discussion about:

1. We found it strange that authors operationalised what are essentially (binary) classification tasks as regression problems; although the network output is pushed through a sigmoidal nonlinearity with a [0--1] range, here this output is never interpreted as a class probability; indeed, instead of maximizing the cross-entropy loss (i.e. maximising the data likelihood) as is normally done in such a context, the authors chose to minimise a squared error loss; this forced them to introduce somewhat arbitrary "target" outputs (0.25 and 0.75) for the two categories. Several questions arise from this odd choice:

a) why did the authors do that? (e.g. is this standard in the NTK literature?)

b) do the results depend on this choice? robustness to this choice is not a priori obvious to us, because the network is not regularised here (see point 2 below), and learning operates in the vastly overparameterised regime where the cross-entropy loss may (does?) not even have a minimum, so weights could diverge. We suspect this may be the answer to (a), but it would be great to discuss this briefly.

2. The paper does not consider generalisation at all, and indeed the tasks studied here are set up in a way that does not even allow thinking about generalisation; the inputs are chosen completely randomly, as opposed to randomly on some category-specific manifold that could be re-sampled, so it is not even clear how a test set would be constructed. Is this an issue? Does that limit the relevance of this study to only a subset of previously studied relevant neuroscience tasks? Again it would be great to discuss.

3. It was not clear to us how much of the results presented here depend on doing gradient descent, as opposed to more generally minimising the loss? This question was apparently already asked as "Comment 2" in the first round of reviews but we found that the rebuttal did not really answer it, beyond saying that solutions are degenerate.

4. After l311, would it be possible to give the intuition for the emergence of context selectivity, in a couple of sentences? The text currently says that it is a "signature of gradient descent" and that the "mechanism is described in detail in Methods 5.6", but we wonder if the authors could be a bit more specific without getting too technical. It is important because the emergence of context selectivity is the most unexpected of the results presented here.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

– The methods section seems very long to me, maybe too long for a general audience. I would strongly suggest focusing on the details and derivations that are necessary to reproduce the results and to understand the main findings. The rest (as beautiful as it is), I would put in the supplementary material (if eLife allows for it).

– Do you need both u and w to be plastic? Have you tried to keep one set fixed? Is the system underdetermined? You show how the cat or ctx selectivity depends on the ratio of learning rates but I am not completely sure which set of weights is the crucial one or let's say the dominant one that is strictly necessary to get the results.

– I am a bit confused how you implemented the context. The stimulus and the context are linearly combined to yield the total sensory input x. But from the perspective of the network that is not different from the simple task. The network sees an input vector x. Whether x is a vector representing the stimulus alone or the stimulus and a context is indistinguishable to the network. Is the difference here that the stimuli were random and orthogonal and if they are linearly combined with another set that is random and orthogonal, the resulting vectors do not necessarily share the same properties? Maybe I misunderstand something here. Would be great if you could clarify that and maybe highlight the differences in the text.

– Maybe worth discussing in the Discussion (these are merely suggestions, I don't expect the authors to run simulations on that):

– comment on limitations and – if possible – how you envision your results to change (or hold) in E/I networks (that abide by Dale's principle) and/or recurrent connections are included.

– How strongly depend the results (or which results) on the gradient descent you used?

– How would the results generalise to more than 2 categories? And what is with the option „unclassified" (no mapping possible).

– I assume each neuron in x is projecting to all neurons in y. Is this clearly stated somewhere? Maybe I missed it – sorry it is hot today!

– After learning, cat selectivity, and later ctx selectivity, cover a broad range with many neurons being close to zero and some showing positive selectivity. However, most of them are still unselective it seems. Is this range in line with experimental results? Could you comment on this heterogeneity? In line 95/96 you say that the cat selectivity increases for EACH neuron but to me it seems some neurons remain at zero selectivity, do I read the figure wrong?

– The distribution of the cat selectivity between the two tasks is different. The cat selectivity for the context-dependent task has many cells with a selectivity close to zero or even negative. Could you comment on that. I apologise if I overlooked it.

claims.claim: The ability to associate sensory stimuli with abstract classes is critical for survival.
claims.source: The ability to associate sensory stimuli with abstract classes is critical for survival.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement drawing from established understanding in neuroscience and evolutionary biology about the importance of categorization for survival.

claims.claim: Experiments have probed two kinds of associations between stimuli and categories: fixed associations and flexible ones.
claims.source: Such experiments have probed two kinds of associations between stimuli and categories: fixed associations (Freedman and Assad, 2006; Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Cromer et al., 2010) (in which, e.g., stimuli are either in category A or in category B), and flexible ones (Wallis et al., 2001; Stoet and Snyder, 2004; Roy et al., 2010; Reinert et al., 2021) (in which, e.g., stimuli are in category A in one context and category B in another).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies that investigated these two types of associations.

claims.claim: Activity of single neurons in associative cortex develops selectivity to task-relevant abstract variables such as category and context during learning.
claims.source: A consistent finding in these experiments is that activity of single neurons in associative cortex develops selectivity to task-relevant abstract variables, such as category (Freedman et al., 2001; Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Reinert et al., 2021) and context (White and Wise, 1999; Wallis et al., 2001; Stoet and Snyder, 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple experimental studies showing selectivity development.

claims.claim: Neurons in visual cortex encode simple sensory variables via negatively correlated responses.
claims.source: Classical work indicates that neurons in visual cortex encode simple sensory variables (e.g., two opposite orientations) via negatively correlated responses (Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; Olshausen and Field, 2004): neurons that respond strongly to a given variable respond weakly to the other one, and vice versa.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classical studies in visual cortex.

claims.claim: Responses in visual cortex to different sensory variables are symmetric.
claims.source: Those responses, furthermore, are symmetric (DeAngelis and Uka, 2003): about the same number of neurons respond strongly to one variable, or the other.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claims.claim: Evidence for negatively correlated and symmetric responses to abstract variables has been reported in monkeys and mice prefrontal cortex.
claims.source: Evidence in favour of this type of responses has been reported in monkeys (White and Wise, 1999; Cromer et al., 2010; Roy et al., 2010; Freedman and Miller, 2008) and mice (Reinert et al., 2021) prefrontal cortex (PFC).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies in PFC.

claims.claim: Responses to categories A and B in monkey lateral intraparietal cortex were found to be positively correlated and strongly asymmetric.
claims.source: However, evidence in favour of a different type of responses has been reported in a different set of experiments from monkeys lateral intraparietal (LIP) cortex (Fitzgerald et al., 2013). In that case, responses to categories A and B were found to be positively correlated: neurons that learn to respond strongly to category A also respond strongly to category B, and neurons that learn to respond weakly to category A also respond weakly to category B. Furthermore, responses were strongly asymmetric: almost all neurons displayed the strongest response to the same category (despite monkeys did not display behavioural biases towards one category or the other).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work in LIP cortex.

claims.claim: The model hypothesizes that synaptic connectivity in neural circuits evolves by implementing gradient descent on an error function.
claims.source: To this end, we hypothesize that synaptic connectivity in neural circuits evolves by implementing gradient descent on an error function (Richards et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors as the basis for their model, with citation to related work.

claims.claim: Under gradient-descent plasticity, neural networks can achieve high performance on both simple and complex tasks.
claims.source: A large body of work has demonstrated that, under gradient-descent plasticity, neural networks can achieve high performance on both simple and complex tasks (LeCun et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to machine learning literature.

claims.claim: Gradient-descent learning can be implemented in a biologically plausible way.
claims.source: Recent studies have furthermore shown that gradient-descent learning can be implemented, at least approximately, in a biologically plausible way (Lillicrap et al., 2016; Whittington and Bogacz, 2017; Sacramento et al., 2018; Akrout et al., 2019; Payeur et al., 2021; Pogodin and Latham, 2020; Boopathy and Fiete, 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent theoretical studies.

claims.claim: The model can capture experimental findings showing that neurons become selective to category and context after learning.
claims.source: Via mathematical analysis and simulations, we show that the model can capture the experimental findings discussed above. In particular, after learning, neurons in the model become selective to category and, if present, context; this result is robust, and independent of the details of the circuit and the task.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' mathematical analysis and simulations presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Whether correlations after learning are positive or negative depends on circuit and task details.
claims.source: On the other hand, whether correlations after learning are positive or negative, and whether population tuning to different categories is asymmetric or not, is not uniquely determined, but depends on details.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' analysis showing parameter dependence.

claims.claim: Activity measures in the model are modulated by circuit details including activation function, learning rates, and initial connectivity.
claims.source: We determined how, in the model, activity measures are modulated by circuit details (activation function of single neurons, learning rates, initial connectivity) and task features (number of stimuli, and whether or not the associations are context dependent).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' systematic analysis of parameter effects.

claims.claim: The circuit model consists of a sensory input layer, an intermediate layer, and a readout neuron.
claims.source: The circuit consists of a sensory input layer (), an intermediate layer (x), and a readout neuron (y). The intermediate (z) and readout (u) weights evolve under gradient descent plasticity (wEquation 1).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: In the simple categorization task, half the stimuli are associated with category A and the other half with category B.
claims.source: In the simple categorization task, half the stimuli are associated with category A and the other half with B.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the task structure shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: In the context-dependent task, associations are reversed across contexts.
claims.source: In the context-dependent task, associations are reversed across contexts: stimuli associated with category A in context 1 are associated with category B in context 2, and vice versa.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the task structure shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Before learning, the category selectivity index is zero on average.
claims.source: Before learning, the responses of single neurons to different stimuli are random and unstructured. Thus, responses to stimuli paired with category A are statistically indistinguishable from responses to stimuli paired with category B (Figure 2A). This makes the category selectivity index zero on average (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claims.claim: After learning, the category selectivity index for most neurons increases.
claims.source: After learning, the responses of single neurons depend on category: within-category responses become more similar than across-category responses, resulting in two separate distributions (Figure 2E). As a consequence, the category selectivity index for most neuron increases; correspondingly, average selectivity increases from zero to positive values (Figure 2F), thus reproducing the behaviour observed in experimental studies (Freedman et al., 2001; Freedman and Assad, 2006; Reinert et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2E and 2F, and is consistent with cited experimental studies.

claims.claim: The selectivity increase is a universal property observed in all circuit models that successfully learned the task, independent of parameters.
claims.source: To determine whether this effect is robust, we varied the parameters that describe the task (number of stimuli) and the biophysical properties of the circuit (the threshold and gain of neurons, Figure 1C, and the learning rates of the two sets of synaptic weights, ηu and ηw). We found that the selectivity increase is a universal property – it is observed in all circuit models that successfully learned the task, independent of the parameters.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by systematic parameter variation in simulations.

claims.claim: Before learning, activity in response to different stimuli is uncorrelated.
claims.source: As discussed above, before learning the responses of neurons in the intermediate layer are random and unstructured. Thus, activity in response to different stimuli is uncorrelated; this is illustrated in Figure 2C, where all non-diagonal entries of the correlation matrix are close to zero.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation matrix shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Over learning, the correlation matrices develop category-dependent structure.
claims.source: Over learning, the correlation matrices develop structure. Correlations become different within the two diagonal, and the two off-diagonal blocks, indicating that learning induces category-dependent structure.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation matrices shown in Figure 2G and 2K.

claims.claim: The model can produce both negative and positive category correlations depending on model details.
claims.source: In Figure 2G, the average correlation within the off-diagonal blocks is negative; the category correlation is thus negative (Cromer et al., 2010; Roy et al., 2010; Freedman and Miller, 2008). The model does not, however, always produce negative correlation: varying model details – either the parameters of the circuit or the number of stimuli – can switch the category correlation from negative to positive (Fitzgerald et al., 2013; one example is shown in Figure 2K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2G and 2K, and is consistent with cited experimental studies.

claims.claim: When category correlation is negative, changes in single-neuron responses to categories A and B have opposite sign.
claims.source: In Figure 2H, where the category correlation is negative, the cloud has a negative slope. This is because changes in single-neuron responses to categories A and B have opposite sign: a neuron that increases its activity in response to category A decreases its activity in response to category B (Figure 2E left), and vice versa (Figure 2E right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of Figure 2H and 2E.

claims.claim: When category correlation is positive, changes in single-neuron responses to categories A and B have the same sign.
claims.source: In Figure 2L, where the category correlation is positive, the cloud has, instead, a positive slope. Here, changes in single-neuron responses to categories A and B have the same sign: a neuron that increases its activity in response to category A also increases its activity in response to category B (Figure 2I, left), and similarly for a decrease (Figure 2I, right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of Figure 2L and 2I.

claims.claim: Over learning, all activity vectors acquire a component aligned with a common, stimulus-independent direction.
claims.source: Over learning, activity vectors in Figure 3A move. Specifically, over learning all activity vectors acquire a component that is aligned with a common, stimulus-independent direction. Activity after learning can thus be approximated by ys≃y0s+csd where y0s indicates initial activity in response to sensory input s, and d indicates the common direction along which activity acquires structure.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical analysis and illustrated in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The coefficients cs are determined by category: approximately equal to cA for category A and cB for category B.
claims.source: The coefficients cs, which measure the strength of the components along the common direction d, are determined by category: they are approximately equal to cA if the sensory input is associated with category A, and cB otherwise.
claims.evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis of the model.

claims.claim: Activity forms two distinct clouds over learning, one for each category.
claims.source: Consequently, over learning, activity vectors associated with different categories are pushed apart along d; this is illustrated in Figure 3B, C, which show activity for the two circuits analyzed in the second and third column of Figure 2, respectively. Activity thus forms two distinct clouds, one for each category; the centers of the two clouds along d are given, approximately, by cA and cB.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the geometric analysis illustrated in Figure 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: The increase in category selectivity is a robust byproduct of gradient-descent learning.
claims.source: The generality of Equation 4 indicates that the increase in selectivity is a robust byproduct of gradient-descent learning, and so can be observed in any circuit that learns the categorization task, regardless of model details.
claims.evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis showing the generality of the result.

claims.claim: Category correlation depends on the threshold and gain of the readout neuron.
claims.source: In Figure 4A, we show category correlation as a function of the threshold and gain of the readout neuron (Figure 1C). We find that varying those can change the magnitude and sign of correlations, with positive correlations favoured by large values of the threshold and gain and negative correlations favoured by small values.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Category correlation is affected by the threshold and gain of neurons in the intermediate layer.
claims.source: Category correlation is also affected by the threshold and gain of neurons in the intermediate layer. This can be seen in Figure 4B, which shows that larger values of the threshold and gain tend to favour positive correlation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Increasing the ratio of learning rates ηw/ηu causes category correlation to decrease.
claims.source: An equally important role is played by the relative learning rates of the the readout, w, and the intermediate weights, u. As illustrated in Figure 4C, increasing the ratio of the learning rates, ηw/ηu, causes the correlation to decrease.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Increasing the number of stimuli causes a systematic decrease in category correlation.
claims.source: Category correlation also depends on the total number of stimuli, a property of the task rather than the circuit (Materials and methods Simple task: category correlation, Equation 77). This is illustrated in Figure 4D, which shows that increasing the number of stimuli causes a systematic decrease in correlation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The model predicts that increasing the number of stimuli should push category correlation from positive to negative values.
claims.source: The model thus makes the experimentally testable prediction that increasing the number of stimuli should push category correlation from positive to negative values.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model's behavior with respect to stimulus number.

claims.claim: Only neurons that are initially strongly connected to the readout neuron exhibit a large selectivity index.
claims.source: Mathematical analysis (see Materials and methods Simple task: computing activity, especially Equation 55) indicates that, for the current task, the category direction d is approximately aligned with the vector that specifies connectivity between the intermediate and the readout neurons, w, before learning starts; we denote this vector w0 (Figure 3B, C). As a consequence, only neurons that are initially strongly connected to the readout neuron – that is, neurons for which w0,i is large – exhibit a large selectivity index (Figure 5B, C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical analysis and simulation results shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claims.claim: The learning algorithm is characterized by inertia, relying on initial connectivity structure more than learned changes.
claims.source: The fact that activity changes are mostly aligned with w0 indicates that the learning algorithm is characterized by a sort of inertia, which makes it rely on initial connectivity structure much more heavily than on the learned one.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the mathematical analysis results.

claims.claim: Changes in selectivity are determined by the strength of synaptic connections a neuron makes to downstream readout areas before learning.
claims.source: In terms of biological circuits, Figure 5 predicts that changes in selectivity are determined by the strength of synaptic connections a neuron makes, before learning, to downstream readout areas.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Experiments in rodents PFC found that neurons highly selective to an abstract variable projected to the same downstream area.
claims.source: Experiments consistent with this prediction have been recently reported: studies in rodents PFC (Ye et al., 2016; Hirokawa et al., 2019) found that all neurons which were highly selective to a given abstract variable were characterized by similar downstream projections (i.e., they projected to the same area).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: In the context-dependent task, average category selectivity increases over learning.
claims.source: Before learning, activity is characterized by small selectivity, which is weakly negative on average (Figure 6A; the fact that average category selectivity is initially weakly negative is due to the composite nature of inputs for this task, see Materials and methods Detailed analysis of category selectivity). Over learning, the average category selectivity increases (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6A and 6D.

claims.claim: The increase in category selectivity in the context-dependent task is highly robust and does not depend on model details.
claims.source: We tested the robustness of this behaviour by varying the parameters that control both the circuit (threshold and gain of neurons, learning rates) and task (number of stimuli and context cues). As in the simple task, we found that the average category selectivity increases in all circuit models, regardless of the parameters (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by systematic parameter variation in simulations.

claims.claim: Average context selectivity increases over learning in the context-dependent task.
claims.source: For this we measure context selectivity which, analogously to category selectivity, quantifies the extent to which single-neuron activity is more similar within than across contexts (Materials and methods Context-dependent task: category and context selectivity, Equation 122). Context selectivity is shown in Figure 6B, E. We find, as we did for category selectivity, that average context selectivity increases over learning – a behaviour that is in agreement with experimental findings (Wallis et al., 2001; Stoet and Snyder, 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6B and 6E, and is consistent with cited experimental studies.

claims.claim: The increase in context selectivity is highly robust and does not depend on model details.
claims.source: The increase in context selectivity is, as for category, highly robust, and does not depend on model details (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by systematic parameter variation in simulations.

claims.claim: Context correlation can either decrease or increase over learning depending on circuit parameters.
claims.source: To quantify this, we focus on the off-diagonal blocks (pairs of trials from different contexts) and measure the average of those correlations, which we refer to as context correlation. Context correlation behaves differently in the two circuits displayed in Figure 6F and I: it decreases over learning in Figure 6F, whereas it increases in Figure 6I.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6F and 6I.

claims.claim: In the context-dependent task, activity forms four clouds, one for each combination of category and context.
claims.source: As in the simple task (Figure 3B, C), activity vectors get re-arranged into statistically distinguishable clouds. While in the simple task clouds were determined by category, here each cloud is associated with a combination of category and context. As a result, four clouds are formed: the cloud of orange circles corresponds to category A and context 1; orange squares to category A and context 2; blue circles to category B and context 1; and blue squares to category B and context 2.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the geometric analysis illustrated in Figure 7B and 7C.

claims.claim: Activity clustering occurs along two directions: one for category (dcat) and one for context (dctx).
claims.source: The transition from unstructured activity (Figure 7A) to four clouds of activity (Figure 7B, C) occurs by learning-induced movement along two directions: dcat, which corresponds to category, and dctx, which corresponds to context.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the geometric analysis illustrated in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The emergence of context-related structure is a signature of the gradient-descent learning rule.
claims.source: The emergence of context-related structure is, on the other hand, more surprising, since the activity of the readout neuron does not depend on context. Nevertheless, context-dependent structure, in the form of clustering, emerges in the intermediate layer activity. Such novel structure is a signature of the gradient-descent learning rule used by the circuit (Canatar et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' analysis and citation to related work.

claims.claim: Context clustering emerges because how similarly intermediate-layer representations evolve is determined by both target category and correlations.
claims.source: But, roughly speaking, context clustering emerges because, for a pair of sensory inputs, how similarly their intermediate-layer representations evolve during learning is determined both by their target category and their correlations (Equation 27, Materials and methods Evolution of connectivity and activity in large circuits).
claims.evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis of the model.

claims.claim: Context correlation depends on the threshold and gain of neurons, relative learning rate, and number of stimuli.
claims.source: In Figure 7D–F, we show how context correlation depends on model parameters. This dependence is qualitatively similar to that of category correlation in the simple task: context correlation depends on the threshold and gain of neurons (compare Figure 7D and Figure 4A), on the relative learning rate ηw/ηu (compare Figure 7E and Figure 4C), and on the number of stimuli (compare Figure 7F and Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7D-F.

claims.claim: The parameter region leading to increased correlation shrinks substantially in the context-dependent task compared to the simple task.
claims.source: However, we find that the region of parameter space leading to an increase in correlation shrinks substantially compared to the simple task (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C, see also Materials and methods Context-dependent task: computing activity); this is in line with the observation that correlations decrease to negative values when the complexity of the task increases, as shown in Figure 4D.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Both category and context directions (dcat and dctx) are strongly correlated with the initial readout vector w0.
claims.source: Analysis in Materials and methods Analysis of patterns of context and category selectivity shows that both the category and context directions, dcat and dctx, are strongly correlated with the initial readout vector w0.
claims.evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis.

claims.claim: Neurons that strongly increase selectivity to either category or context are strongly connected to the downstream readout neuron before learning.
claims.source: As in the simple task, this leads to the prediction that neurons that strongly increase selectivity to either category or context are, before learning, strongly connected to the downstream readout neuron (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model analysis and shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: Among strongly selective neurons, some develop mixed selectivity to category and context, others develop pure selectivity to category, but none develop pure selectivity to context.
claims.source: In Figure 8B, we plot changes in context selectivity as a function of changes in category selectivity. We observe that, among all the neurons that strongly increase their selectivity, some increase selectivity to both category and context (orange sample neuron), and others increase selectivity to category, but not context (yellow sample neuron). In contrast, none increases selectivity to context but not category.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: The model predicts that neurons with pure selectivity to category and mixed selectivity to category and context should be observed, but neurons with pure selectivity to context should not.
claims.source: This makes the following experimental prediction: among all the neurons that are strongly connected to the readout, neurons with pure selectivity to category and neurons with mixed selectivity to category and context should be observed, but neurons with pure selectivity to context should not.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model analysis.

claims.claim: The asymmetry between category and context arises because the readout neuron learns to read out category but not context.
claims.source: The asymmetry between category and context arises because, in the model, the readout neuron learns to read out category, but not context.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation derived from the model structure.

claims.claim: When a second readout neuron that learns to read out context is included, neurons with strong pure selectivity to context are also observed.
claims.source: We show in Figure 6—figure supplement 3E, F that if a second readout neuron, which learns to read out context, is included in the circuit, neurons with strong pure selectivity to context are also observed.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3E, F.

claims.claim: Pure- and mixed-selective neurons are characterized by different patterns of initial response gain.
claims.source: Analysis reported in Materials and methods Analysis of patterns of context and category selectivity indicates that these two populations are characterized by different properties of the initial activity. In particular, the two populations are characterized by different initial patterns of the response gain (defined as the slope of the activation function, Figure 1C, at the response), which measures the local sensitivity of neurons to their inputs.
claims.evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis and illustrated in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Initial activity plays an important role in learning by breaking symmetry among neurons and determining functional specialization.
claims.source: Overall, these results indicate that initial activity, which is mostly unstructured and task-agnostic, plays an important role in learning: it breaks the symmetry among neurons in the intermediate layer, and determines which functional specialization neurons will display over learning.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of how initial conditions affect learning outcomes.

claims.claim: The model provides a framework for interpreting seemingly disparate experimental findings.
claims.source: Overall, the model provides a framework for interpreting seemingly disparate experimental findings, and for making novel experimental predictions.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of the work.

claims.claim: The model can recapitulate experimental observations including seemingly disparate ones.
claims.source: We find that the model is able to recapitulate experimental observations, including seemingly disparate ones.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the model's capabilities based on the analyses presented.

claims.claim: The dependencies of activity measures on circuit and task details make experimentally testable predictions.
claims.source: These dependencies make experimentally testable predictions about the circuitry supporting abstract knowledge acquisition in the brain.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the predictive value of the model.

results.result: The model robustly reproduces the experimental finding that neurons develop selectivity to task-relevant abstract variables (category and context) during learning, independent of circuit and task parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C17-C19, C28, C38-C41 collectively demonstrate that category and context selectivity increase over learning across all parameter regimes tested. The mathematical analysis (C28) shows this is a general property of gradient-descent learning, and simulations (C17-C19, C38-C41) confirm robustness across varied circuit parameters and task complexity. This is consistent with cited experimental studies.

results.result: The sign and magnitude of category and context correlations depend on circuit parameters (activation function properties, learning rate ratios) and task features (number of stimuli, task complexity), with the model producing both negative and positive correlations depending on these details.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C20-C24, C29-C32, C42, C47-C48 demonstrate through mathematical analysis and simulations that correlation behavior is parameter-dependent. The model successfully reproduces both negatively correlated symmetric responses (observed in PFC) and positively correlated asymmetric responses (observed in LIP cortex), with specific dependencies on circuit and task parameters quantified in Figures 4 and 7.

results.result: Activity evolution during learning can be geometrically characterized as movement along stimulus-independent directions, forming distinct clusters for different categories (simple task) or category-context combinations (context-dependent task).
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27, C43-C44 describe the geometric structure of activity changes, supported by mathematical analysis (Equations 3, 29) and visualizations (Figures 3, 7). The clustering structure emerges naturally from gradient-descent learning and explains the selectivity increases. The mathematical framework provides closed-form expressions for the clustering directions and coefficients.

results.result: Neurons that develop strong selectivity are those initially strongly connected to downstream readout neurons, with the clustering directions correlated with initial readout connectivity (w0).
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36, C49-C50 establish the relationship between initial connectivity and selectivity changes through mathematical analysis (Equations 55, 65) and simulations (Figures 5, 8A). The 'inertia' property of learning in large networks causes activity changes to align with initial readout weights. This prediction is consistent with cited experimental observations in rodent PFC.

results.result: In the context-dependent task, neurons develop either mixed selectivity (category and context) or pure category selectivity, but not pure context selectivity, with this pattern determined by initial activity properties and readout architecture.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C56 describe the distribution of selectivity types, supported by simulations (Figure 8B) and mathematical analysis (Equations 172, 181). The asymmetry arises because only category is read out. When a second readout for context is added (C54), pure context selectivity emerges, confirming the mechanistic explanation. Initial response gain patterns distinguish the two populations (C55, Figure 8C).

results.result: Context-dependent structure emerges in the intermediate layer even though the readout neuron does not depend on context, as a signature of gradient-descent learning driven by input correlations.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 explain the surprising emergence of context clustering through the gradient-descent learning rule. The mathematical analysis (Equation 27) shows that representation evolution depends on both target category and input correlations. This is supported by simulations showing four-cluster structure (Figure 7) and is consistent with cited work on gradient-descent signatures.

results.result: The model predicts that increasing the number of stimuli should push category correlation from positive to negative values.
results.evaluation: Claim C33 makes a testable prediction based on the systematic analysis in Figure 4D and Equation 77. The mathematical framework shows that correlation decreases with stimulus number, and this is verified in simulations. This represents a novel, experimentally testable prediction that could distinguish between different brain regions or task conditions.

results.result: The model is based on the hypothesis that synaptic connectivity evolves via gradient descent, which can be implemented in biologically plausible ways and achieves high performance on tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10 establish the modeling framework with appropriate citations to prior work. C8 states the hypothesis clearly, C9 cites machine learning evidence for performance, and C10 cites recent theoretical work on biological plausibility. These provide the foundation for the model but are not novel contributions of this work.

results.result: Prior experimental work has established that neurons develop selectivity to abstract variables during categorization learning, with different brain regions showing different correlation patterns (negative/symmetric in PFC, positive/asymmetric in LIP).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 summarize prior experimental findings with appropriate citations. These establish the empirical context and apparent discrepancies that motivate the modeling work. The citations appear accurate and the characterization of prior findings is consistent with the cited literature.

results.result: The model architecture consists of a three-layer feedforward circuit learning two categorization tasks: a simple linearly separable task and a context-dependent nonlinearly separable task.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 describe the model architecture and tasks, illustrated in Figure 1. This is a straightforward description of the modeling setup. The architecture is standard and the task definitions are clear and appropriate for testing the hypotheses.

results.result: The model provides a unified framework for interpreting disparate experimental findings and makes experimentally testable predictions about how circuit and task details modulate neural representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C57-C59 summarize the overall contribution of the work. These are supported by the comprehensive analysis of parameter dependencies (Figures 4, 7) and the specific predictions made (C33, C36, C52). The framework successfully reconciles seemingly contradictory experimental observations through parameter variation.

results.result: Recent experiments in rodent PFC found that highly selective neurons project to the same downstream area, consistent with the model's prediction.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 cites experimental evidence (Ye et al., 2016; Hirokawa et al., 2019) that is consistent with the model's prediction about initial connectivity determining selectivity. However, the authors note that full validation would require additional measurements (correlation between connection strength and selectivity), which have not yet been performed.

results.result: The model demonstrates that neurons develop robust selectivity to task-relevant abstract variables (category and context) after learning through gradient descent. This selectivity increase is universal across all parameter settings and independent of circuit or task details.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding, stating the paper 'provides compelling evidence that neural networks trained on two-way classification tasks will develop responses whose category and context selectivity profiles depend on key network details.' The robustness of selectivity increases is not questioned, though reviewers request clarification about the dependence on gradient descent specifically.

results.result: The model shows that category and context correlations (positive vs. negative) depend on specific circuit parameters including activation function thresholds and gains, learning rate ratios, and task features like stimulus number. The model can produce both positive and negative correlations depending on these parameters.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this as a key contribution, noting the paper provides 'compelling evidence' that selectivity profiles 'depend on key network details, such as neural activation functions and initial connectivity.' They recognize these results 'can explain apparently contradictory results in the experimental literature.'

results.result: The model demonstrates that learning reorganizes neural activity into distinct clouds in activity space, with activity vectors acquiring components along common stimulus-independent directions determined by category (and context in the context-dependent task).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this geometric interpretation of learning dynamics. They accept the mathematical framework and request only more intuitive explanations of the mechanisms, particularly for context selectivity emergence, indicating acceptance of the underlying results.

results.result: The emergence of context-related structure in the intermediate layer is a signature of gradient-descent learning, occurring even though the readout neuron does not depend on context. This emerges because intermediate-layer representations evolve based on both target category and input correlations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly request clarification about this result, asking 'would it be possible to give the intuition for the emergence of context selectivity, in a couple of sentences?' and noting 'it is important because the emergence of context selectivity is the most unexpected of the results.' They also question 'how much of the results presented here depend on doing gradient descent, as opposed to more generally minimising the loss?'

results.result: The model predicts that neurons developing strong selectivity are those initially strongly connected to downstream readout neurons before learning. The learning algorithm exhibits 'inertia,' relying heavily on initial connectivity structure rather than learned changes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these predictions about the role of initial connectivity. They accept the framework and request discussion about generalization and model choices, but do not question the specific findings about initial connectivity determining selectivity changes.

results.result: The model predicts an asymmetry between category and context selectivity: neurons with pure category selectivity and mixed selectivity should be observed, but not neurons with pure context selectivity (unless a context readout is included). This asymmetry arises from the readout structure, and initial activity patterns determine functional specialization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recognize these as 'new experimental predictions for testing in the future' and do not challenge the logic or findings. They accept the model's predictive framework, though they request discussion about generalization to more complex scenarios.

results.result: The model makes experimentally testable predictions, including that increasing stimulus number should push category correlation from positive to negative values, and provides predictions about circuitry supporting abstract knowledge acquisition.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the predictive value, stating the results 'make new experimental predictions for testing in the future.' They recognize the paper's contribution to interpreting experimental findings and generating testable hypotheses.

results.result: The model is based on the hypothesis that synaptic connectivity evolves through gradient descent on an error function, which can be implemented in biologically plausible ways and enables high performance on tasks.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly question the dependence on gradient descent, asking 'how much of the results presented here depend on doing gradient descent, as opposed to more generally minimising the loss?' They note this question was 'apparently already asked' in a previous review round and 'the rebuttal did not really answer it.' This indicates uncertainty about whether gradient descent specifically is necessary.

results.result: The model architecture consists of a sensory input layer, intermediate layer, and readout neuron, with two types of tasks: simple categorization (fixed stimulus-category associations) and context-dependent (reversed associations across contexts).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the model architecture itself. Reviewer 2 requests clarification about context implementation ('I am a bit confused how you implemented the context'), but this is a request for explanation rather than a challenge to the validity of the approach.

results.result: Background claims establishing that neurons in associative cortex develop selectivity to abstract variables during learning, with different studies reporting both negatively correlated/symmetric responses (PFC) and positively correlated/asymmetric responses (LIP cortex).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these as established experimental findings that motivate the study. They recognize the paper addresses 'apparently contradictory results in the experimental literature,' implicitly accepting the characterization of existing experimental observations.

results.result: Experimental studies in rodent PFC found that highly selective neurons projected to the same downstream area, consistent with the model's predictions about initial connectivity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this supporting experimental evidence. They accept the paper's framework for relating model predictions to existing experimental findings.

results.result: Before learning, neural responses are random and uncorrelated. After learning, correlation matrices develop category-dependent structure, with the sign of correlations (positive or negative) determining whether neurons show same-sign or opposite-sign changes in responses to different categories.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these characterizations of pre- and post-learning activity patterns. They accept the correlation analysis framework and focus their questions on interpretation and generalization rather than the validity of these observations.

results.result: The model provides a framework for interpreting seemingly disparate experimental findings and can recapitulate experimental observations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this contribution, stating 'The findings of the paper are very valuable for neuroscientists studying the learning of abstract representations' and that results 'can explain apparently contradictory results in the experimental literature.'

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations support the finding that category and context selectivity increase over learning across parameter regimes (C11, C18, C19, C28, C38-C41). OpenEval emphasizes mathematical analysis and robustness, while peer reviewers request clarification about dependence on gradient descent specifically. OpenEval includes C17 which peer reviewers address separately in R12.

Both strongly support the parameter-dependent correlation behavior (C12, C22, C29-C32, C42, C47-C48). Peer reviewers explicitly recognize this as 'compelling evidence' that explains contradictory experimental results. OpenEval includes additional claims C20-C21, C23-C24 that peer reviewers address in R12.

Perfect agreement on geometric structure of activity changes (C25-C27, C43-C44). Both accept the mathematical framework and clustering structure. Peer reviewers request more intuitive explanations but do not challenge the underlying results.

Both support the relationship between initial connectivity and selectivity changes (C34-C36, C49-C50). OpenEval emphasizes the 'inertia' property and experimental consistency. Peer reviewers accept the framework without challenging specific findings, requesting only discussion about generalization.

Both support the distribution of selectivity types and asymmetry findings (C51-C56). OpenEval provides detailed mechanistic explanation. Peer reviewers recognize these as 'new experimental predictions' without challenging the logic or findings.

Significant disagreement on context selectivity emergence (C45-C46). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with mathematical explanation. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, explicitly requesting intuition and questioning dependence on gradient descent, noting this is 'the most unexpected of the results.'

Both support the testable prediction about correlation decreasing with stimulus number (C33). Peer reviewers explicitly affirm predictive value and recognize contribution to generating testable hypotheses. Peer R7 also includes C59 which OpenEval addresses in R11.

Divergent evaluations of modeling framework (C8-C10). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, viewing these as appropriate foundation claims. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, explicitly questioning whether gradient descent specifically is necessary versus general loss minimization, noting this question was not adequately answered in previous review.

Both support the characterization of prior experimental findings (C1-C7). OpenEval emphasizes appropriate citations and consistency with literature. Peer reviewers accept these as established findings that motivate the study.

Both support the model architecture and task descriptions (C14-C16). OpenEval views as straightforward setup. Peer reviewers request clarification about context implementation but do not challenge validity of the approach.

Both support the overall contribution claims (C13, C57-C59 for OpenEval; C57-C58 for peer). OpenEval emphasizes comprehensive parameter analysis. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm findings are 'very valuable for neuroscientists' and explain contradictory experimental results. OpenEval includes C13 and C59 not in peer R13.

Both support the experimental evidence about initial connectivity (C37). OpenEval notes that full validation requires additional measurements not yet performed. Peer reviewers accept the framework for relating predictions to existing findings without challenge.

Peer reviewers separately evaluate pre- and post-learning activity patterns (C17, C20-C21, C23-C24) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval includes these claims within broader evaluations R1 and R2 rather than as a distinct result about correlation analysis framework.
